items.summary: Iran praises Houthi victory along strategic Red Sea coast as ‘divine triumph’ Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has congratulated Yemen’s Houthis following reports of them seizing the entire Red Sea coastline of the country. The advance was described by IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi as a “divine triumph” and the culmination of years of resistance by the group. The Houthis’ advance represents a “divine triumph and the fruit of years of steadfastness in the most difficult of battlefields”, Mohebi wrote on X. Iranian officials have continued to hail the Houthi gains. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said that “the homegrown resolve of the resistance have driven the US and its allies into a tactical and strategic impasse”.

items.title: Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city, sources say
items.summary: Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city, sources say The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in US-Israeli war on Iran, according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources. Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close US ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said. Several senior Revolutionary Guards commanders had already travelled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks directed against Saudi Arabia after weeks of discussions over military strategy, a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said. A third Iranian source, an official, said Iran had held several meetings with allies including the Houthis and that the move on Mocha was a Houthi rather than Iranian decision. However, it had helped Iran by putting upward pressure on oil prices and hurting the United States and Saudi Arabia, the official added. Reporting by Reuters

The security of Islam's two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a "red line", coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early on Wednesday, adding that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the Houthis. items.title: Saudi Arabian pipeline outage threatens global oil supply
items.summary: Saudi Arabian pipeline outage threatens global oil supply Saudi Arabia will run out of oil stocks for exports if it doesn't restart its major pipeline to the Red Sea within days, leading to a loss of up to 4 percent of global supply, Saudi oil buyers and traders told Reuters on Sunday. A further decline in Saudi flows will worsen the global supply crunch, which has already pushed global fuel prices to record highs since the start of the US-Iran war. Following the drone attacks launched from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to shut its huge East-West oil pipeline on Friday, Riyadh has not given full details about the extent of the damage or how long the route will stay offline. Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying estimates, with one saying the damage could take as long as five to six weeks to repair, while another said it could be fixed sooner and could resume pumping partially while repairs are ongoing.

items.summary: US opposes Iran nuclear chief attending IAEA conference The United States opposed the head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organisation attending the annual conference of the UN nuclear watchdog, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday. Speaking to reporters in Vienna, where the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is based, Wright said Mohammad Eslami was subject to US sanctions and had been denied a request for a waiver. “He’s a sanctioned individual and we don’t want sanctioned individuals evading their sanctions. He asked for a waiver of the sanctions and it was denied,” Wright said. Eslami has regularly attended and addressed the IAEA General Conference since becoming head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organisation in 2021. Iranian state television said Eslami and a delegation travelled to Vienna on a regular flight Saturday but were “blocked on the way because of obstructions by the United States”.

Located at the centre of the Bab al-Mandab Strait,  Mayyun Island is a key monitoring point overlooking the vital maritime passage. Two Yemeni sources also told Reuters that Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had withdrawn from Perim Island. The development came after Houthis seized the western coastal city of Mocha, forcing the government forces to retreat toward the south and the city of Dhubab. The Sanaa-based Yemen Press Agency, citing field sources, said Houthi forces seized the al-Omari camp overlooking the strait. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree was also reported as saying that navigation in the Red Sea was safe except for Saudi ships, suggesting the group now has control over the Strait of Mandeb. items.summary: IRGC claims attacks on oil tankers, ships and US vessels Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted several vessels that attempted to pass through what it described as the "forbidden and unsafe area" of ​​the Strait of Hormuz. According to the IRGC's latest statement, its navy attacked and "caused great damage" to two American vessels and eight oil tankers in retaliation to earlier US strikes on Iranian vessels. It also targeted 10 "violating ships", that it said were "attempting to pass through the prohibited and unsafe area of ​​the Strait of Hormuz, with the instigation and support of the invading terrorist army of the United States". "The Strait of Hormuz is under the strong and powerful surveillance and management of the capable and brave naval force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps," it added.

items.title: Tehran condemns US attacks on Iranian commercial vessels
items.summary: Tehran condemns US attacks on Iranian commercial vessels Iran’s foreign ministry has condemned a US attack on Iranian commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman on Saturday. In a statement, the ministry said the strikes were “a continuation of the US military aggression against Iran”, adding that it constituted a "clear violation" of a clause in the "United Nations Charter, a war crime, and an overt threat to international peace and the security of commercial shipping". The ministry asserted that Tehran remains determined to "firmly defend its sovereignty and national interests" against US actions, including Washington's ongoing maritime blockade, attacks on commercial vessels, and its continued "economic war". "The Ministry of Foreign Affairs stresses that responsibility for the consequences arising from the continuation of US aggressive and interventionist actions in the region will rest with the US regime and its accomplices and partners," it added.

items.title: Houthi attacks expose gaps in Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Houthi attacks expose gaps in Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia After positioning itself as a regional mediator by facilitating talks between Washington and Tehran, Pakistan marked a major milestone in its expanding diplomacy last month: the signing of a trilateral defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey in Islam’s holiest city. Signed in Mecca on 7 August, the Joint Defence Agreement states that an attack on one signatory will be treated as an attack on all, drawing immediate comparisons to Nato’s Article 5, even as analysts cautioned against taking the clause too literally. That commitment was quickly tested on 8 September, when Iran-backed Houthi forces launched a massive drone and missile barrage into Saudi Arabia, striking critical military and energy infrastructure. Overnight, an abstract commitment turned into a high-stakes operational question. Neither Islamabad nor Ankara launched military counter-operations alongside Riyadh, choosing firm diplomatic statements instead. Read more: Houthi attacks expose gaps in Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia Left to right

The US Defense Department’s inspector general released the first report on the war with Iran, covering 1 April through 30 June. According to the Pentagon watchdog, munitions expenditure during the war "has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply". To mitigate the constraints, the report said that the Pentagon is "working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times and to stockpile critical materials, components and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency". US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have repeatedly denied media reports over depleted arms stockpiles. These rapid changes have pushed Yemen’s war back into the regional arena, threatening Red Sea shipping and placing the country’s Saudi-backed, internationally-recognized government on the back foot. The rapid reversal came only days after the government declared a campaign to retake Sanaa, Yemen’s capital, amid a broader escalation in fighting across the country. items.title: The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial
items.summary: The extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait. The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate , a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. items.summary: Trump downplays report China supplied satellite images aiding Jordan base attack US president Donald Trump brushed aside a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops there in July. A recent report in the Wall Street Journal cited unnamed US officials about the attack in Jordan. Asked whether he would mention the issue at an upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump did not directly answer, and instead equated the surveillance activities of China and the US. "They basically do what we do," he told reporters aboard Air Force One. "When they say China spies on us, I say you're right and we spy on them too." The East-West Pipeline has become increasingly important for Saudi Arabia during the Iran war, enabling state oil giant Aramco to ship crude from the kingdom’s eastern coast to the Red Sea on its western coast. items.title: Iranian strikes damaged multiple aircraft at Jordan base, report says
items.summary: Iranian strikes damaged multiple aircraft at Jordan base, report says Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a US official told Reuters. The US military, the highest-funded in the world, suffered material damage even before Iran's strikes on Tuesday. This includes the destruction of more than two dozen drones, Iran striking fighter jets, and aircraft being lost to accidents. According to a May report from the Congressional Research Service, 42 US military aircraft had already been lost or damaged in the conflict. Since the Iran war started in February, 18 US service members have been killed and over 800 injured. A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Iran's attack hit one A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, leaving it with a missing wing, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and were returned to service. Iran's strike on the US base in Jordan came after US forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. Report by Reuters

items.summary: Trump advisers warn Iran conflict could stretch through his term, WSJ reports Top White House advisers, including vice president JD Vance and secretary of state Marco Rubio, have privately warned president Donald Trump that the conflict with Iran could extend through the remainder of his presidency, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing US officials. The White House did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The advisers told Trump in private discussions in the Oval Office and the Situation Room that Tehran could continue to resist US pressure, potentially prolonging the conflict beyond Inauguration Day in January 2029, the Journal added. The reported warning contrasts with Trump's own public remarks about the war. The president said on Wednesday he expected the war to end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November, arguing that Iran was trying to influence the vote but would be unable to sustain its resistance much longer. Trump also acknowledged diplomatic talks are still a possibility but were not preferred. Report by Reuters

"I think the war will end immediately after the election" because Iran "can't hold out any longer," Trump told journalists, accusing Tehran of being "desperate to try and affect" the vote. Asked about the possibility of resumed talks with Tehran, Trump said "we’re not looking for it, to be honest", adding that "they have very little country left right now", but "a negotiation could possibly happen". He also reiterated his intention to prohibit Iran from having nuclear weapons.

items.summary: Iran war cost hits $38bn, forecast to rise $3bn a month, CBO says The six-month-old US war on Iran has cost $38bn so far, and that amount is projected to rise by $3bn a month, Congress's nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ways to end the war and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz. The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5 percent in the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office accounting, which totalled expenses through 1 August. The mounting costs have strained US munitions stockpiles and driven up energy prices, adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.

items.title: Houthis say Saudi Arabia launched over 50 strikes against them in 24 hours
items.summary: Houthis say Saudi Arabia launched over 50 strikes against them in 24 hours Yemen's Houthis said Sunday that Saudi Arabia had launched more than 50 strikes against their positions in 24 hours, after the group claimed a rare drone and missile attack on a military base in the kingdom. The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with Saudi-backed government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea. The latest clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing Yemen's Red Sea coast, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The waterway is a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the Iran war.

items.title: Iraq eyes Europe as it seeks to diversify oil exports
items.summary: Iraq eyes Europe as it seeks to diversify oil exports Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said on Tuesday that he discussed selling oil to Europe during visits to France and Germany, as Baghdad seeks to diversify its export routes and reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz. During a press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin, Zaidi said "we want to expand and diversify our export routes". He added that "Iraq cannot remain hostage to a single corridor" as recent events have demonstrated, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blockaded by Iran during the war. Zaidi said that he had discussed oil exports to Europe with Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, whom he met in Paris on Monday.

Speaking to heads of the country’s leading universities, Pezeshkian said universities should support the government across areas including the economy, management, culture and literature, ISNA reported. Pezeshkian also called for greater involvement of students in tackling national issues. “We must make sure that instead of engaging in protest, they engage in solving problems,” he said. items.summary: Underwater drone capture gives Tehran opportunity to reverse engineer vessel Iran's capture of a US military underwater drone gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse engineer the vessel, delivering a setback for the Pentagon and drone maker Anduril. The US military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands. The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention. Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter. After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then-President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design. clusters.headline: How Congress gave up its power over war and peace

items.title: How Congress gave up its power over war and peace
items.summary: In 1973, after it was discovered that the U.S. had secretly bombed Cambodia, Congress took action. In an effort to assert its power over matters of war and peace, Congress pushed through the War Powers Resolution despite then-President Richard Nixon’s veto, and it has been law ever since. Unfortunately, congressional enforcement of the War Powers Resolution has been mixed. In 2026 alone, Congress has put forward some 19 war powers resolutions in an attempt to rein in hostilities in Iran, Venezuela, Cuba, and Lebanon. So far, none of these resolutions has stopped a conflict. Take Iran, for example. There have been eight votes to end the war, seven of which failed. Just one of these passed and only because Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) changed course after losing his primary to a challenger endorsed by President Donald Trump, giving him leeway to vote against the bulk of the Republican Party. Cassidy’s move highlights one of the main problems with the War Powers Resolution: too many of our elected officials cast votes for political gain, not American interests. items.title: Trump's govt makes 'treasonous' claim of weapons shortages
items.summary: In the last two days, a pair of government reports confirmed what many outside analysts have claimed: the Iran war has been extraordinarily costly for the U.S. military and for the American public. A Congressional Budget Office (CBO) analysis released Tuesday afternoon found that the Iran war has already cost the Department of Defense (DoD) $38 billion. While this is significantly lower than the $100-billion-plus price tag independent experts have calculated, CBO notes that its estimates were limited because “DoD did not respond to CBO’s requests for information.” Without help from the DoD, CBO could not include a number of known war costs in its analysis, including repairing damage to U.S. military bases in the region. Those costs alone could top $200 billion , according to experts. What CBO could confirm was that the war has been a disaster for the U.S. economy and military readiness. The CBO analysis estimates that the inflation rate is now expected to be a full half-point higher in 2027 than it was before the war began, almost entirely because of higher global energy costs result

clusters.headline: Massie tells RS why he went after Hegseth and not Trump

items.title: Massie tells RS why he went after Hegseth and not Trump
items.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) tells Responsible Statecraft that he is initiating eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth because Congress has “exhausted every other remedy to make things right.” After a speech on the floor Tuesday, Massie said is forcing a vote on the articles in the House, which would likely happen on Thursday before the chamber recesses for the midterms. The resolution is quite a brief against Hegseth, covering U.S. military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela, as well as accusing Hegseth of minimizing civilian deaths and abridging freedom of speech. Impeachment votes are privileged in the House, which means the measure can bypass the rules and go straight to a floor vote after debate. The articles would have to get a motion, however, which would require a majority vote. It is not clear how many Democrats would vote for it. Democrats just killed a resolution to impeach President Donald Trump by one of their own , Rep. Al Green (D-Texas). We spoke to Massie on Tuesday. items.title: Iran war cost US $38bn and significantly depleted missile stockpile, report finds
items.summary: Damaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuild The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found, in a damaging report less than two months before midterm elections where the war and the cost of living crisis will likely hurt Republicans at the polls. The economic report comes one day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. items.summary: A viral selfie allegedly showing Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping, Narendra Modi and other leaders together at the BRICS summit in New Delhi is AI-generated. A SynthID watermark shows it was created using OpenAI tools, while several leaders pictured, including Brazil’s Lula and Turkey’s Erdogan, did not attend. Another AI selfie features former Iranian president Ebrahim Raisi, who died in 2024. Both images were widely shared online, including by official embassy accounts. Vedika Bahl fact-checks.

items.summary: Iran gebruikt spionagesoftware om gevoelige informatie te verzamelen over kritische Iraniërs die in het Westen wonen. Daarvoor waarschuwt de Nederlandse inlichtingendienst AIVD, samen met de Amerikaanse FBI en het Britse cybersecuritycentrum NCSC. Iraanse diensten proberen via sociale media contact te leggen met dissidenten, activisten en journalisten en hun vertrouwen te winnen. Daarna vragen de Iraanse "cyberactoren" hen om een bestand te downloaden en dat te openen, zeggen de diensten. 'Volledige controle' Zodra het bestand is geopend heeft de software, Chosen Brick, volgens de AIVD "volledige controle over het apparaat". Zo kan het Iraanse regime toegang krijgen tot contactpersonen, e-mails en socialemedia-accounts van het slachtoffer. Ook kan de software beveiligingsinstellingen aanpassen of die in- of uitschakelen en schermafbeeldingen maken. Vooral apparaten van Windows zouden het doelwit zijn. In augustus ging het CPB ervan uit dat een doorsnee huishouden er volgend jaar 0,3 procent op achteruitgaat in koopkracht. Door de maatregelen die op Prinsjesdag zijn aangekondigd is de raming nu een achteruitgang van 0,1 procent voor het doorsnee huishouden. Plusje voor laagste inkomens Alleen de laagste inkomens gaan er volgend jaar iets op vooruit: +0,2 procent. En gepensioneerden: +0,3 procent. Gepensioneerden krijgen er geld bij doordat pensioenfondsen er goed voorstaan en daardoor de pensioenen kunnen verhogen. De koopkracht van de laagste inkomens groeit een beetje doordat werkenden een grotere korting krijgen op hun inkomstenbelasting. "Er gebeurt wel iets om voor bepaalde groepen de koopkracht iets op te krikken", zegt CPB-directeur Pieter Hasekamp. "Het kabinet heeft ervoor gekozen om werkenden een steuntje in de rug te geven door die arbeidskorting iets te verhogen." items.summary: Last week, the war in Ukraine reached deep inside the Russian Arctic. On September 9, Ukrainian drones struck two gas processing plants in the Yamalo-Nenets region, located about 1,900 miles from the Ukrainian border. This is Ukraine’s deepest strike on Russia since the war began. Arctic energy infrastructure in the Yamal region produces around 80% of Russia's natural gas. Russian military analysts believe the Ukrainian drones were launched from Sumy, northern Ukraine, and reached all the way into Yamal with the help of Starlink. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces announced , “Until today, this was considered an absolutely safe rear.” The attack also shook European energy markets, as Europe buys large volumes of gas from the Yamal region. President Donald Trump later told Ukraine to stop attacking Russia’s diesel infrastructure, saying fuel shortages due to the strikes were “hurting the world,” without explicitly acknowledging the fact that the spike in global energy prices is largely driven by the Iran war. clusters.headline: Planbureau ziet klimaatbeleid vastlopen: 'Enorme kloof tussen ambitie en beleid'

items.title: Planbureau ziet klimaatbeleid vastlopen: 'Enorme kloof tussen ambitie en beleid'
items.summary: De uitstoot van gassen die de aarde opwarmen daalt niet meer, klimaatdoelen zijn ver buiten bereik en ons land blijft voor energie nog jaren afhankelijk van gas, steenkool en olie uit het buitenland. Dat stelt het Planbureau voor de Leefomgeving (PBL) vast in een rapport over het klimaat- en energiebeleid dat jaarlijks verschijnt rond Prinsjesdag. Hoewel die conclusies niet erg anders zijn dan voorgaande jaren , klinken de onderzoekers steeds bezorgder. De aanpak van klimaatverandering zou vastlopen, en zonder nieuwe plannen gaat ons land de zichzelf gestelde doelen niet halen. Op deze koers mist ons land waarschijnlijk zijn streefdoel voor 2030. En komt niet in de buurt van de ambities voor de tientallen jaren erna. "We geven drie jaar op rij al aan dat de kans dat we het doel voor 2030 halen heel erg klein is", zegt Marko Hekkert, directeur van het PBL. "Dit jaar hebben we voor het eerst gekeken naar 2040. Wat je ziet is echt een enorme kloof tussen de ambitie aan de ene kant en het beleid aan de andere kant. Dat is nieuwe informatie waar het kabinet echt rekenschap van moet geven.

clusters.headline: Austria says ‘lack of consensus’ at UN led to ban on Iran nuclear chief

items.title: Austria says ‘lack of consensus’ at UN led to ban on Iran nuclear chief
items.summary: Austria says ‘lack of consensus’ at UN led to ban on Iran nuclear chief Austria said on Monday that a decision to exclude Iran’s nuclear chief, Mohammad Eslami, from entering the country to attend the annual meeting of the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna was because there was no consensus at the UN Security Council. Austria’s foreign ministry said it had requested an exemption to a current UN travel ban on Eslami but was denied. “Austria, as the host country of the International Atomic Energy Agency, applied to the relevant committee of the United Nations Security Council for an exemption from the existing UN travel ban for Mr Mohammed Eslami,” the ministry said. “Subsequently, Austria was informed by the president of the United Nations Security Council that the request had been rejected due to a lack of consensus. Entry could therefore not be permitted in view of Austria’s international obligations,” it added. “Austria wants to make negotiations in Vienna possible. We do so on the basis of international law and our international obligations.”

items.title: European business survey – Bridging the gap between geopolitics and corporate strategy
items.summary: Geopolitical uncertainty has made economic security a central issue on the EU agenda. Companies are playing a crucial role in reducing strategic dependencies, strengthening resilience and diversifying supply chains. A pilot survey of 228 companies operating in Europe offers initial insights into how businesses assess geopolitical risks and what they expect from EU policymakers. The survey was conducted between November 2025 and January 2026 – several years into the Sino-US trade and tech conflict, the Ukrainian war, and supply chain concerns that emerged especially after the Covid-crisis but before recent escalations in transatlantic relations and the Iran conflict. Around 130–150 respondents answered the majority of the survey questions.

items.summary: Iran blacklists 77 ships accused of breaking Strait of Hormuz rules Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority has placed 77 vessels on a list of ships it accuses of “violating Iranian protocols for the Strait of Hormuz”. The Iranian body, which oversees transit requests through the waterway, said the vessels could face “fines, detention or confiscation” if they attempt future crossings. It warned that it would also list commercial ships that cooperate with the US and its allies. Tehran disputes repeated assertions by US President Donald Trump that the American military exercises “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran says it will not reopen the strait until Washington meets its demands over US attacks, reparations and sanctions.

items.summary: Forget the bombing: the Trump administration keeps insisting this isn’t a war. items.title: Iran says agreement with Oman would not mean the reopening of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran says agreement with Oman would not mean the reopening of Hormuz Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Sunday that Iran's anticipated agreement with Oman to govern the Strait of Hormuz will not trigger a reopening of the waterway. In comments to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, Araghchi said Iran will provide details of the agreement and the new route maps to countries participating in a meeting with Gulf states in the Omani capital tomorrow, adding that the agreement does not “in any way” signal that the strait will reopen, which is conditional on the US honouring its commitments under the Memorandum of Understanding signed in Islamabad, he said. “Iran believes that the responsibility for ensuring security and stability in the region lies solely with the countries of the region,” Araghchi added.

items.summary: Government insiders say the new PM is unleashing an ‘earthquake’ to clean up the system. But Iraqis have heard it all before The gates of the Green Zone in Baghdad are made of five-metre-high armoured steel, reinforced with horizontal girders, and strung between concrete pillars and anti-blast walls. Police water cannon trucks are stationed nearby, along with armoured personnel carriers and squads of heavily armed soldiers. At the first sign of street protests – over failing electricity, unemployment or, more recently, the US-Israeli attacks on Iran – the gates are shut. X-shaped vehicle barriers, made from welded iron beams and mounted on wheels, sit ready at the roadside alongside coils of razor wire; both are slid across the street, sealing off the sprawling neighbourhood, home to the presidential palace, parliament, the prime minister’s office, the massive fortress-like US embassy, and other institutions, including the homes of scores of politicians and members of parliament. Dat meldt het Indiase ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken na een ontmoeting tussen de Indiase premier Narendra Modi en de Chinese president Xi Jinping. De twee spraken elkaar vandaag op de BRICS-top in New Delhi. Het ministerie verklaarde na de ontmoeting dat "de twee leiders zich hebben uitgesproken voor een eerlijke, redelijke en voor beide partijen aanvaardbare oplossing". Al decennia speelt tussen China en India een conflict over de grens die dwars door het Himalaya-gebergte loopt. In 2020 was daar nog een militaire confrontatie. Twintig Indiase en vier Chinese militairen sneuvelden daarbij. De betrekkingen tussen de twee landen zijn sindsdien weer verbeterd, maar aan beide kanten van de 3500 kilometer lange grens is er nog altijd een forse militaire aanwezigheid. clusters.headline: Brics backs Gaza ceasefire, calls for two-state solution for Palestine

items.title: Brics backs Gaza ceasefire, calls for two-state solution for Palestine
items.summary: Brics backs Gaza ceasefire, calls for two-state solution for Palestine Brics leaders on Saturday adopted a joint declaration calling for the extension of the “ceasefire” in Gaza and backing a two-state solution for Palestine. The declaration said root causes of conflicts must be tackled and reiterated the group's commitment to peaceful resolution through “dialogue, consultation and diplomacy”. The group, which comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, also raised concerns over the increasing nuclear risks and emphasised that nuclear safeguards, safety and security must be upheld, including in armed conflicts. The Brics leaders also praised the “ceasefire” in Lebanon and urged the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which calls for the cessation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. The declaration also condemned unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, saying they distort trade and violate World Trade Organisation rules.

clusters.headline: Opinion: 9/11 at 25: Has the US learned anything from its 'war on terror'?

items.title: Opinion: 9/11 at 25: Has the US learned anything from its 'war on terror'?
items.summary: Opinion: 9/11 at 25: Has the US learned anything from its 'war on terror'? A quarter century is enough time to separate history from hysteria, consequences from intentions and reality from propaganda. On 11 September 2001, nearly 3,000 people were killed in horrific attacks that shocked the United States and the world. The attacks of 9/11 could have been treated as a grave crime requiring an international effort to identify, apprehend and prosecute those responsible. They could also have triggered a serious national debate about why such intense hostility towards the US had developed in many parts of the Muslim-majority world. Instead, the US's political establishment chose a radically different path. President George W Bush famously declared that the terrorists attacked the US because "they hate our freedoms". It was a convenient explanation because it absolved the American foreign policy establishment of any responsibility. items.summary: US sanctions Iraqi paramilitary group Kataib Hezbollah The United States has imposed sanctions targeting Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned Iraqi paramilitary group, as part of an effort to disrupt financial networks supporting Iran’s regional activities, the US State Department said. “Today, the United States is taking action under Operation Economic Outcast targeting Kata’ib Hizballah (KH), Hizballah, and the broader financial networks that sustain Iran’s campaign of regional destabilization,” State Department spokesman Thomas Pigott said. Pigott said the group and those linked to it serve as Iran’s “instruments for projecting violence and subversion across the Middle East”. Kataib Hezbollah has rejected an Iraqi government order requiring paramilitary groups to disarm.

After days of heavy fighting along a narrow plain known as the Tihama, on Thursday the Houthis routed Yemeni forces loyal to Saudi Arabia and seized the historic and strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha. items.summary: La respuesta de Irán a la guerra lanzada por Donald Trump y Benjamin Netanyahu tiene muchas formas y se extiende al mar Rojo. Los iraníes han convertido Ormuz en su arma más importante de presión y los hutíes, sus aliados yemeníes, se suman de lleno al conflicto con la captura del puerto de Moka, la entrada al estrecho de Bab El Mandeb (que se traduce del árabe como 'la puerta de las lágrimas'). Ormuz es la puerta energética del Golfo; Bab el Mandeb, la del mar Rojo y el Canal de Suez, una ruta clave del comercio entre Asia y Europa y punto de paso de alrededor del 7 por ciento del petróleo mundial. Y esto solo parece un primer paso, porque los hutíes avanzan para hacerse con el control total de la costa. La ofensiva de los rebeldes sorprendió a las fuerzas del Gobierno, que cuentan con el respaldo de Arabia Saudí, pero apenas ofrecieron resistencia lo que muestra su mala organización. En menos de una semana, los hutíes han tomado amplias partes del país y los bombardeos saudíes no han podido frenar a sus unidades terrestres, que avanzan en vehículos todoterreno y motocicletas. items.summary: De Houthi's in Jemen hebben de havenstad Mokka ingenomen. Dat meldt persbureau Reuters, op basis van militaire bronnen van de Jemenitische regering. De inname van de stad markeert de grootste verschuiving van de frontlinies in vier jaar tijd. Vorige week begonnen de Houthi's, die worden gesteund door Iran, een offensief met vermoedelijk als doel om controle te krijgen over Bab el-Mandeb, de belangrijke zeestraat tussen Jemen en de Hoorn van Afrika. In de afgelopen dagen wonnen de Houthi's al flink terrein, met onder meer de herovering van de stad Hais, gisternacht. Niet ver daarvandaan ligt de stad Mokka. Vanochtend verschenen de eerste beelden vanuit de stad. Op beelden die de NOS verifieerde zijn onder meer Houthi-strijdkrachten te zien bij een verlaten voertuig van het Jemenitische staatsleger. Wie zijn de Houthi's? Dat en vier andere vragen leggen we in dit artikel aan je uit. Mokka is een strategisch gelegen havenstad aan de Rode Zee, iets ten noorden van de zeestraat. items.summary: Olivier Grondeau a passé deux ans et demi en prison en Iran. Son nom est moins connu que ceux d’otages dont le cas a été médiatisé. Son histoire est assez proche. Arrêté à Chiraz le 12 octobre 2022, à l’époque des manifestations suivant la mort de Jina Mahsa Amini, il a été libéré en mars 2025. Il n’avait décidé de parler de sa situation que quelques mois plus tôt. Olivier Grondeau est un voyageur à tout petit budget, un poète, un grand lecteur, un ancien champion de scrabble. C’est son esprit, son humour, son imagination qui l’ont aidé à tenir. Il le raconte dans un livre publié chez l’iconoclaste : « Joseph dans la nuit »

items.title: Political Instability Meets Fiscal Limits: Is France the Euro’s Next Big Stress Test?
items.summary: With around half a year remaining before the next presidential election, France is in danger of becoming a stress test for the eurozone: a political crisis, a deteriorating fiscal position and growing market doubts about the country’s ability to finance its mounting debt burden are all converging. France faces a significant structural imbalance in its public finances. The budget deficit exceeds 5 per cent of GDP , while public expenditure stands at around 57 per cent of GDP. At the same time, public debt is rising steadily and could, without sufficient fiscal consolidation measures, exceed 130 per cent of GDP by 2030 . The interest burden on public debt is rising rapidly and could rise to more than 120 billion euros, equivalent to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2030. The central challenge, however, may not lie in the fiscal arithmetic of the budget, but in the political capacity to address it. items.title: Symposium: What I miss most about pre-9/11 America
items.summary: While it is somewhat cliche to say that the “whole world changed” after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks on the United States, it does not detract from the reality of the statement. In numerous tangible ways, the culture, security, and politics of the nation were never the same after al-Qaida hijackers in passenger planes left nearly 3,000 people dead in smoldering ruins across lower Manhattan, the Pentagon, and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. For many of us who lived through it all, a quarter century has passed in a blink, while at the same time the pre-9/11 Washington era paradoxically seems so far away, and perhaps softened a bit by wistfulness and nostalgia. Conversely, the “post” era is pockmarked by wars, and an expansion of the national security state that was unimaginable a generation ago. Those born too early to witness the events of that day know nothing other than the current atmosphere of hyper-securitization and political polarization. It wouldn’t be an exaggeration to say 9/11 and the “Global War on Terror” that followed are somewhere at the root of these woes. RS aske

Front-month Brent crude futures settled up $3.29, or 3.4%, at $101.21 a barrel, after touching a high of $101.58. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude was up $3.02, or 3.25%, at $96.05 a barrel. items.title: Dodental na luchtaanval op Houthi-gevangenis in Jemen loopt op tot 23
items.summary: Bij een luchtaanval op een gevangenis in het noorden van Jemen zijn zeker 23 mensen om het leven gekomen. Reddingswerkers hebben vandaag vier lichamen geborgen uit het puin van de gevangenis, die maandag instortte na een aanval van de door Saudi-Arabië geleide coalitie. De gevangenis stond in de strategisch gelegen stad Hazm, in de provincie Jawf. Volgens de Houthi's wordt nog gezocht naar zeven vermisten. Bij de aanval raakten zeker zeven mensen gewond. Onder hen was een vrouw die haar echtgenoot in de gevangenis bezocht. De identiteit van de dodelijke slachtoffers is nog niet vastgesteld. De aanval maakt deel uit van een nieuwe escalatie van het conflict in Jemen. De door Saudi-Arabië geleide coalitie voerde vanochtend nieuwe luchtaanvallen uit op militaire doelen van de Houthi's in de provincies Marib en Jawf. De Houthi's reageerden eerder met een reeks raket- en droneaanvallen op het zuiden van Saudi-Arabië. Daarbij raakten volgens de autoriteiten 73 mensen gewond. items.summary: Shallah, Fatimah and Maahi are among hundreds of thousands of Afghan women and girls deported from Iran and Pakistan in the past year to a life of severe restrictions It was a warm summer afternoon on 15 August 2021 when the Taliban entered Kabul and changed the lives of millions. Shallah*, then 16, watched the news at home on the Afghan TV channel Tolo news. She ran crying to the garden, to tell her mother that Afghanistan had fallen. Her younger sister, Fatimah*, then 11, was at her cousin’s house, where her aunt told her the news. At the time, she says, she did not understand what a takeover meant, or who the Taliban were. Her elder sister, Maahi*, then 22, was well aware of the consequences and remembers her hands shaking at work as she read the news on her phone, on Facebook pages of Afghan news. Continue reading...

clusters.headline: Vat olie boven de 100 dollar, ook benzineprijs blijft stijgen

items.title: Vat olie boven de 100 dollar, ook benzineprijs blijft stijgen
items.summary: Na de nieuwe aanvallen van de Verenigde Staten en Iran zijn de olieprijzen opnieuw gestegen. De prijs van een vat Brent-olie kwam vanochtend boven de 100 dollar uit. Dat is voor het eerst sinds juli. Een vat Brent-olie is inmiddels bijna 60 procent duurder dan begin dit jaar. Door de aanvallen tussen de Verenigde Staten en Iran is er onrust op de oliemarkt. Het aanhoudende geweld vergroot de zorgen over mogelijke verstoringen van de olie-export uit de regio. De Amerikaanse bank Goldman Sachs heeft gewaarschuwd dat de olieprijs kan oplopen naar 120 dollar per vat als de aanvallen aanhouden. De stijgende olieprijs is ook al te merken aan de pomp. De adviesprijs voor een liter benzine ligt nu rond de 2,72 euro.

clusters.headline: Transition énergétique: la facture de l'après-pétrole sera lourde pour les pétro-États

items.title: Transition énergétique: la facture de l'après-pétrole sera lourde pour les pétro-États
items.summary: La sortie mondiale du pétrole pourrait entraîner des conflits, des migrations et des bouleversements économiques selon une étude du groupe de réflexion E3G publiée mardi 8 septembre. L’utilisation du pétrole est en déclin dans de nombreux pays, avec la croissance des énergies renouvelables, et les effets de la guerre en Iran qui a limité l’offre et fait flamber les prix. Et cette stagnation va obliger les producteurs à rechercher un bassin d’acheteurs en déclin. Des pays comme le Nigeria, l’Iran, l’Angola et l’Algérie font partie des pays qui seront gravement touchés, car ils dépendent fortement des revenus pétroliers pour financer leurs services publics. Sans aide internationale, ils ne pourront pas amortir le choc alertent les experts.

These include everything from his seeming “war on DEI” within the department, to combative engagements with members of Congress, to shade being thrown even by President Donald Trump himself on the lack of success in the (second) Iran War. items.summary: Trying to pin the blame for the depletion of U.S. military stockpiles on something other than the war in Iran, President Donald Trump fell back on a usual scapegoat last week: Ukraine. “The Biden administration gave far more munitions away to Ukraine, at no cost to them whatsoever, than we have used in Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. This is a familiar refrain. Trump loves to remind his audience that because of him, Americans are “not spending on Ukraine anymore” and instead, Europe is footing the bill. In truth, most people in the United States don’t think about Ukraine much these days. But since Trump himself brought it up, it’s worth asking: What exactly is going on with U.S. military support to Ukraine? The answer might surprise you. Despite Trump’s rhetoric, the United States remains deeply embroiled in Ukraine’s ongoing conflict with Russia in ways that create national security risks and run counter to Trump’s own foreign policy goals. items.summary: Twenty-five years ago, 19 hijackers took control of four American airliners and crashed them into symbols of American power, killing upwards of 3000 people. The American population watched the events unfold in real time. It was an emotionally jarring event that changed the country. In some respects, the events of 9/11 needed no explanation. The destruction of the World Trade Center buildings and the massive, and random, loss of life were horrifying to all. The meaning of the attacks, however – and the motivations of the hijackers – were less clear. The effort to explain the motives behind the attack, and to understand “why they hate us,” brought a pre-existing debate over Islamist militancy to the center of American public life. In the decade leading up to 9/11, the Washington policy community had been divided over how to deal with the Islamist movement and particularly those extremists who sought to use violence to impose a narrow vision of religious orthodoxy upon reluctant societies. items.title: Somali piracy was under control. Then came the Iran war.
items.summary: From the start, the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran has been a story of unintended consequences. Contrary to President Donald Trump’s hopes for a quick victory, the conflict has morphed into a sustained crisis, one that has driven up oil prices, driven down tourism in the Middle East, and reshaped the region’s geopolitical map. Now, a new unintended consequence has emerged: the return of piracy to Somalia’s coasts. This shift, which comes after a decade of quiet, threatens some of the world’s most important shipping lanes and the interests of the United States and its allies. Pirates have attacked at least 15 vessels in the region this year, a sharp uptick from the five attacks that occurred last year, according to data from the International Maritime Organization. The renewed criminal activity has led to extended hostage situations, including one ongoing seizure of an oil tanker and its crew. clusters.headline: US strikes perimeter of Iran’s Bushehr nuclear plant, Iranian state media reports

items.title: US strikes perimeter of Iran’s Bushehr nuclear plant, Iranian state media reports
items.summary: US strikes perimeter of Iran’s Bushehr nuclear plant, Iranian state media reports The United States targeted the perimeter of Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant on Thursday, Iranian state media reported, citing Ehsan Jahanian, deputy governor of Bushehr province. Jahanian said several areas across the province were targeted, including the area around the nuclear plant, a military base in the town of Choghadak and a fishing pier in southern Bushehr. He said there were no immediate reports of casualties. Residents in Choghadak, located just over 20km (12 miles) from the Bushehr plant, reported hearing several explosions. The Bushehr facility, Iran’s only civilian nuclear power plant, has previously been affected by strikes in the area during the ongoing Middle East war.

items.summary: IAEA chief says renewed access to Iran nuclear sites could have ‘positive repercussions’ Rafael Grossi, the chief of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), said on Monday that restoring its access to key facilities in Iran could have “very, very positive repercussions” for Tehran, as the US, Britain, France and Germany prepare to seek a resolution referring Iran to the UN Security Council. The IAEA has been unable to access several key Iranian nuclear sites since Israel, later joined by the US, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear facilities. Sites have also been hit in the latest war, which began on 28 February, prompting repeated calls from the agency for renewed access. “The best, shortest way for a positive outcome is for Iran to engage with us,” Grossi told reporters after opening the IAEA Board of Governors’ quarterly meeting. Grossi said his engagement with Iran would continue regardless of the outcome of the vote, adding that serious dialogue and renewed access to nuclear sites would have significant positive consequences. clusters.headline: Iran warns of retaliation if IAEA adopts resolution against Tehran

items.title: Iran warns of retaliation if IAEA adopts resolution against Tehran
items.summary: Iran warns of retaliation if IAEA adopts resolution against Tehran Iran has warned that it will take reciprocal action if the UN nuclear watchdog adopts a resolution against Tehran, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on Monday. Speaking at a press briefing, Baghaei criticised European states seeking a resolution against Iran, calling their approach “irrational” given that the ongoing US-Iran war has made several Iranian nuclear facilities inaccessible to international inspectors. His comments come as the US, Britain, France and Germany push for a resolution at the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) over Iran’s lack of cooperation and access to its nuclear sites. Iran has restricted IAEA access to facilities affected by previous strikes, arguing that normal safeguarding arrangements have become impractical under wartime conditions. The dispute has deepened concerns over the status of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile and the international community’s ability to verify the nature of its nuclear programme.

But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait. The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate , a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. The security of Islam's two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a "red line", coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early on Wednesday, adding that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the Houthis. Malki described the incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca, following what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch in July 2017. items.title: Trump's govt makes 'treasonous' claim of weapons shortages
items.summary: In the last two days, a pair of government reports confirmed what many outside analysts have claimed: the Iran war has been extraordinarily costly for the U.S. military and for the American public. A Congressional Budget Office (CBO) analysis released Tuesday afternoon found that the Iran war has already cost the Department of Defense (DoD) $38 billion. While this is significantly lower than the $100-billion-plus price tag independent experts have calculated, CBO notes that its estimates were limited because “DoD did not respond to CBO’s requests for information.” Without help from the DoD, CBO could not include a number of known war costs in its analysis, including repairing damage to U.S. military bases in the region. Those costs alone could top $200 billion , according to experts. What CBO could confirm was that the war has been a disaster for the U.S. economy and military readiness. The CBO analysis estimates that the inflation rate is now expected to be a full half-point higher in 2027 than it was before the war began, almost entirely because of higher global energy costs result

items.title: Massie tells RS why he went after Hegseth and not Trump
items.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) tells Responsible Statecraft that he is initiating eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth because Congress has “exhausted every other remedy to make things right.” After a speech on the floor Tuesday, Massie said is forcing a vote on the articles in the House, which would likely happen on Thursday before the chamber recesses for the midterms. The resolution is quite a brief against Hegseth, covering U.S. military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela, as well as accusing Hegseth of minimizing civilian deaths and abridging freedom of speech. Impeachment votes are privileged in the House, which means the measure can bypass the rules and go straight to a floor vote after debate. The articles would have to get a motion, however, which would require a majority vote. It is not clear how many Democrats would vote for it. Democrats just killed a resolution to impeach President Donald Trump by one of their own , Rep. Al Green (D-Texas). We spoke to Massie on Tuesday. The economic report comes one day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. In augustus ging het CPB ervan uit dat een doorsnee huishouden er volgend jaar 0,3 procent op achteruitgaat in koopkracht. Door de maatregelen die op Prinsjesdag zijn aangekondigd is de raming nu een achteruitgang van 0,1 procent voor het doorsnee huishouden. Plusje voor laagste inkomens Alleen de laagste inkomens gaan er volgend jaar iets op vooruit: +0,2 procent. En gepensioneerden: +0,3 procent. Gepensioneerden krijgen er geld bij doordat pensioenfondsen er goed voorstaan en daardoor de pensioenen kunnen verhogen. De koopkracht van de laagste inkomens groeit een beetje doordat werkenden een grotere korting krijgen op hun inkomstenbelasting. "Er gebeurt wel iets om voor bepaalde groepen de koopkracht iets op te krikken", zegt CPB-directeur Pieter Hasekamp. "Het kabinet heeft ervoor gekozen om werkenden een steuntje in de rug te geven door die arbeidskorting iets te verhogen." The US Defense Department’s inspector general released the first report on the war with Iran, covering 1 April through 30 June. items.title: Ukraine war spreads to Arctic as nuclear tensions escalate
items.summary: Last week, the war in Ukraine reached deep inside the Russian Arctic. On September 9, Ukrainian drones struck two gas processing plants in the Yamalo-Nenets region, located about 1,900 miles from the Ukrainian border. This is Ukraine’s deepest strike on Russia since the war began. Arctic energy infrastructure in the Yamal region produces around 80% of Russia's natural gas. Russian military analysts believe the Ukrainian drones were launched from Sumy, northern Ukraine, and reached all the way into Yamal with the help of Starlink. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces announced , “Until today, this was considered an absolutely safe rear.” The attack also shook European energy markets, as Europe buys large volumes of gas from the Yamal region. President Donald Trump later told Ukraine to stop attacking Russia’s diesel infrastructure, saying fuel shortages due to the strikes were “hurting the world,” without explicitly acknowledging the fact that the spike in global energy prices is largely driven by the Iran war. items.title: Houthi attacks expose gaps in Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia

Signed in Mecca on 7 August, the Joint Defence Agreement states that an attack on one signatory will be treated as an attack on all, drawing immediate comparisons to Nato’s Article 5, even as analysts cautioned against taking the clause too literally. That commitment was quickly tested on 8 September, when Iran-backed Houthi forces launched a massive drone and missile barrage into Saudi Arabia, striking critical military and energy infrastructure. Overnight, an abstract commitment turned into a high-stakes operational question. Neither Islamabad nor Ankara launched military counter-operations alongside Riyadh, choosing firm diplomatic statements instead. items.title: Planbureau ziet klimaatbeleid vastlopen: 'Enorme kloof tussen ambitie en beleid'
items.summary: De uitstoot van gassen die de aarde opwarmen daalt niet meer, klimaatdoelen zijn ver buiten bereik en ons land blijft voor energie nog jaren afhankelijk van gas, steenkool en olie uit het buitenland. Dat stelt het Planbureau voor de Leefomgeving (PBL) vast in een rapport over het klimaat- en energiebeleid dat jaarlijks verschijnt rond Prinsjesdag. Hoewel die conclusies niet erg anders zijn dan voorgaande jaren , klinken de onderzoekers steeds bezorgder. De aanpak van klimaatverandering zou vastlopen, en zonder nieuwe plannen gaat ons land de zichzelf gestelde doelen niet halen. Op deze koers mist ons land waarschijnlijk zijn streefdoel voor 2030. En komt niet in de buurt van de ambities voor de tientallen jaren erna. "We geven drie jaar op rij al aan dat de kans dat we het doel voor 2030 halen heel erg klein is", zegt Marko Hekkert, directeur van het PBL. "Dit jaar hebben we voor het eerst gekeken naar 2040. Wat je ziet is echt een enorme kloof tussen de ambitie aan de ene kant en het beleid aan de andere kant. Dat is nieuwe informatie waar het kabinet echt rekenschap van moet geven.

items.title: Austria says ‘lack of consensus’ at UN led to ban on Iran nuclear chief

Austria’s foreign ministry said it had requested an exemption to a current UN travel ban on Eslami but was denied. “Austria, as the host country of the International Atomic Energy Agency, applied to the relevant committee of the United Nations Security Council for an exemption from the existing UN travel ban for Mr Mohammed Eslami,” the ministry said. “Subsequently, Austria was informed by the president of the United Nations Security Council that the request had been rejected due to a lack of consensus. Entry could therefore not be permitted in view of Austria’s international obligations,” it added. “Austria wants to make negotiations in Vienna possible. We do so on the basis of international law and our international obligations.”

items.title: US opposes Iran nuclear chief attending IAEA conference
items.summary: US opposes Iran nuclear chief attending IAEA conference The United States opposed the head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organisation attending the annual conference of the UN nuclear watchdog, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday. Speaking to reporters in Vienna, where the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is based, Wright said Mohammad Eslami was subject to US sanctions and had been denied a request for a waiver. “He’s a sanctioned individual and we don’t want sanctioned individuals evading their sanctions. He asked for a waiver of the sanctions and it was denied,” Wright said. Eslami has regularly attended and addressed the IAEA General Conference since becoming head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organisation in 2021. Iranian state television said Eslami and a delegation travelled to Vienna on a regular flight Saturday but were “blocked on the way because of obstructions by the United States”.

items.title: Boven Iran neergeschoten bemanningslid F-15 vertelt over spectaculaire redding
items.summary: Voor het eerst heeft een van de twee in Iran geredde bemanningsleden van een Amerikaanse F-15 zijn verhaal gedaan. Het toestel van de man werd door Iran neergehaald . Hij had zijn rug, arm en schouder gebroken na een harde landing, maar wist desondanks een groot stuk af te leggen om zich te verbergen. "Ik was gewond, maar we trainen allemaal om met de dingen om te gaan die op ons pad komen", zei het bemanningslid 'Bravo' tegen 60 Minutes . In het interview vertelt hij uitgebreid over het succesverhaal in wat het CBS-televisieprogramma verder een dure en impopulaire oorlog noemt. De echte naam van de man wordt geheim gehouden vanwege dreiging uit Iran. De andere inzittende, piloot Alpha, wilde niet in de uitzending reageren. A further decline in Saudi flows will worsen the global supply crunch, which has already pushed global fuel prices to record highs since the start of the US-Iran war. Following the drone attacks launched from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to shut its huge East-West oil pipeline on Friday, Riyadh has not given full details about the extent of the damage or how long the route will stay offline. Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying estimates, with one saying the damage could take as long as five to six weeks to repair, while another said it could be fixed sooner and could resume pumping partially while repairs are ongoing.

items.title: Making Iraq ‘normal’ again: do mass arrests and cash seizures signal end to corruption?
items.summary: Government insiders say the new PM is unleashing an ‘earthquake’ to clean up the system. But Iraqis have heard it all before The gates of the Green Zone in Baghdad are made of five-metre-high armoured steel, reinforced with horizontal girders, and strung between concrete pillars and anti-blast walls. Police water cannon trucks are stationed nearby, along with armoured personnel carriers and squads of heavily armed soldiers. At the first sign of street protests – over failing electricity, unemployment or, more recently, the US-Israeli attacks on Iran – the gates are shut. X-shaped vehicle barriers, made from welded iron beams and mounted on wheels, sit ready at the roadside alongside coils of razor wire; both are slid across the street, sealing off the sprawling neighbourhood, home to the presidential palace, parliament, the prime minister’s office, the massive fortress-like US embassy, and other institutions, including the homes of scores of politicians and members of parliament. items.summary: China en India willen gezamenlijk toewerken naar een oplossing voor het grensgeschil tussen de twee landen. Dat meldt het Indiase ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken na een ontmoeting tussen de Indiase premier Narendra Modi en de Chinese president Xi Jinping. De twee spraken elkaar vandaag op de BRICS-top in New Delhi. Het ministerie verklaarde na de ontmoeting dat "de twee leiders zich hebben uitgesproken voor een eerlijke, redelijke en voor beide partijen aanvaardbare oplossing". Al decennia speelt tussen China en India een conflict over de grens die dwars door het Himalaya-gebergte loopt. In 2020 was daar nog een militaire confrontatie. Twintig Indiase en vier Chinese militairen sneuvelden daarbij. De betrekkingen tussen de twee landen zijn sindsdien weer verbeterd, maar aan beide kanten van de 3500 kilometer lange grens is er nog altijd een forse militaire aanwezigheid. items.summary: Houthis say liberated more than 200 prisoners in newly captured regions Yemen's Houthis said on Saturday that they had freed more than 200 of their members detained by Saudi-backed pro-government forces in areas they captured in recent days. Houthi official Abdelkader al-Murtada said they were prisoners of war who had spent up to eight years in jail before the Iran-backed group launched a rapid offensive to take over areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab Strait. "We have welcomed 210 of our prisoners, freed from Saudi enemy prisons on the west coast," Murtada said at a conference in the capital Sanaa. items.title: Brics backs Gaza ceasefire, calls for two-state solution for Palestine
items.summary: Brics backs Gaza ceasefire, calls for two-state solution for Palestine Brics leaders on Saturday adopted a joint declaration calling for the extension of the “ceasefire” in Gaza and backing a two-state solution for Palestine. The declaration said root causes of conflicts must be tackled and reiterated the group's commitment to peaceful resolution through “dialogue, consultation and diplomacy”. The group, which comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, also raised concerns over the increasing nuclear risks and emphasised that nuclear safeguards, safety and security must be upheld, including in armed conflicts. The Brics leaders also praised the “ceasefire” in Lebanon and urged the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which calls for the cessation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. The declaration also condemned unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, saying they distort trade and violate World Trade Organisation rules.

items.title: Opinion: 9/11 at 25: Has the US learned anything from its 'war on terror'?
items.summary: Opinion: 9/11 at 25: Has the US learned anything from its 'war on terror'? A quarter century is enough time to separate history from hysteria, consequences from intentions and reality from propaganda. On 11 September 2001, nearly 3,000 people were killed in horrific attacks that shocked the United States and the world. The attacks of 9/11 could have been treated as a grave crime requiring an international effort to identify, apprehend and prosecute those responsible. They could also have triggered a serious national debate about why such intense hostility towards the US had developed in many parts of the Muslim-majority world. Instead, the US's political establishment chose a radically different path. President George W Bush famously declared that the terrorists attacked the US because "they hate our freedoms". It was a convenient explanation because it absolved the American foreign policy establishment of any responsibility. items.title: US diesel prices surpass $6 a gallon for first time as oil hits highest since May
items.summary: US diesel prices surpass $6 a gallon for first time as oil hits highest since May The US national average price of diesel on Thursday surpassed $6 a gallon for the first time ever, according to price tracker GasBuddy, as the US-Israeli war on Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s refineries have squeezed supply. The latest surge in fuel costs is adding to inflationary pressures that have already strained consumers and businesses this year, creating a political headache for President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers as they seek to defend thin congressional majorities in November's midterm elections. Crude oil futures on Thursday hit their highest level since mid-May. Brent settled at $107.63 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate futures at $102.48 a barrel.

Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close US ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said. Several senior Revolutionary Guards commanders had already travelled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks directed against Saudi Arabia after weeks of discussions over military strategy, a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said. A third Iranian source, an official, said Iran had held several meetings with allies including the Houthis and that the move on Mocha was a Houthi rather than Iranian decision. However, it had helped Iran by putting upward pressure on oil prices and hurting the United States and Saudi Arabia, the official added. Reporting by Reuters

The bill, backed by parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, would restrict contacts with foreign media and institutions, the sharing of information, scientific cooperation and other activities that authorities deem to facilitate foreign influence. The elected government's opposition to the measure appears to signal pushback towards hardliners, who have supported enacting tougher security laws during the US-Israeli war on Iran. items.title: Political Instability Meets Fiscal Limits: Is France the Euro’s Next Big Stress Test?
items.summary: With around half a year remaining before the next presidential election, France is in danger of becoming a stress test for the eurozone: a political crisis, a deteriorating fiscal position and growing market doubts about the country’s ability to finance its mounting debt burden are all converging. France faces a significant structural imbalance in its public finances. The budget deficit exceeds 5 per cent of GDP , while public expenditure stands at around 57 per cent of GDP. At the same time, public debt is rising steadily and could, without sufficient fiscal consolidation measures, exceed 130 per cent of GDP by 2030 . The interest burden on public debt is rising rapidly and could rise to more than 120 billion euros, equivalent to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2030. The central challenge, however, may not lie in the fiscal arithmetic of the budget, but in the political capacity to address it. On the one hand, the costs of social welfare expenditure are no longer sustainable; on the other, the majority of the population continues to demand more state intervention. The US military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands. The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention. Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter. After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then-President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design. Symposium: What I miss most about pre-9/11 America
items.summary: While it is somewhat cliche to say that the “whole world changed” after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks on the United States, it does not detract from the reality of the statement. In numerous tangible ways, the culture, security, and politics of the nation were never the same after al-Qaida hijackers in passenger planes left nearly 3,000 people dead in smoldering ruins across lower Manhattan, the Pentagon, and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. For many of us who lived through it all, a quarter century has passed in a blink, while at the same time the pre-9/11 Washington era paradoxically seems so far away, and perhaps softened a bit by wistfulness and nostalgia. Conversely, the “post” era is pockmarked by wars, and an expansion of the national security state that was unimaginable a generation ago. Those born too early to witness the events of that day know nothing other than the current atmosphere of hyper-securitization and political polarization. items.title: Trump advisers warn Iran conflict could stretch through his term, WSJ reports
items.summary: Trump advisers warn Iran conflict could stretch through his term, WSJ reports Top White House advisers, including vice president JD Vance and secretary of state Marco Rubio, have privately warned president Donald Trump that the conflict with Iran could extend through the remainder of his presidency, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing US officials. The White House did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The advisers told Trump in private discussions in the Oval Office and the Situation Room that Tehran could continue to resist US pressure, potentially prolonging the conflict beyond Inauguration Day in January 2029, the Journal added. The reported warning contrasts with Trump's own public remarks about the war. The president said on Wednesday he expected the war to end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November, arguing that Iran was trying to influence the vote but would be unable to sustain its resistance much longer. Trump also acknowledged diplomatic talks are still a possibility but were not preferred. Report by Reuters

items.title: How Congress gave up its power over war and peace
items.summary: In 1973, after it was discovered that the U.S. had secretly bombed Cambodia, Congress took action. In an effort to assert its power over matters of war and peace, Congress pushed through the War Powers Resolution despite then-President Richard Nixon’s veto, and it has been law ever since. Unfortunately, congressional enforcement of the War Powers Resolution has been mixed. In 2026 alone, Congress has put forward some 19 war powers resolutions in an attempt to rein in hostilities in Iran, Venezuela, Cuba, and Lebanon. So far, none of these resolutions has stopped a conflict. Take Iran, for example. There have been eight votes to end the war, seven of which failed. Just one of these passed and only because Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) changed course after losing his primary to a challenger endorsed by President Donald Trump, giving him leeway to vote against the bulk of the Republican Party. Cassidy’s move highlights one of the main problems with the War Powers Resolution: too many of our elected officials cast votes for political gain, not American interests. L’utilisation du pétrole est en déclin dans de nombreux pays, avec la croissance des énergies renouvelables, et les effets de la guerre en Iran qui a limité l’offre et fait flamber les prix. Et cette stagnation va obliger les producteurs à rechercher un bassin d’acheteurs en déclin. Des pays comme le Nigeria, l’Iran, l’Angola et l’Algérie font partie des pays qui seront gravement touchés, car ils dépendent fortement des revenus pétroliers pour financer leurs services publics. Sans aide internationale, ils ne pourront pas amortir le choc alertent les experts.

She frames the war in the Persian Gulf as a mutually damaging stalemate in which neither Washington nor Tehran has found a politically sustainable exit: "There are no winners in this war". Her central argument is that the conflict has created a problem of face-saving as much as military strategy. The US faces rising economic and electoral costs, while Iran confronts shortages, inflation, domestic dissent and intensified repression. Neither side, in her assessment, can plausibly claim success.

items.title: 25 years after 9/11, the US still doesn't know 'why they hate us'
items.summary: Twenty-five years ago, 19 hijackers took control of four American airliners and crashed them into symbols of American power, killing upwards of 3000 people. The American population watched the events unfold in real time. It was an emotionally jarring event that changed the country. In some respects, the events of 9/11 needed no explanation. The destruction of the World Trade Center buildings and the massive, and random, loss of life were horrifying to all. The meaning of the attacks, however – and the motivations of the hijackers – were less clear. Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August : one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey. items.title: US strikes perimeter of Iran’s Bushehr nuclear plant, Iranian state media reports
items.summary: US strikes perimeter of Iran’s Bushehr nuclear plant, Iranian state media reports The United States targeted the perimeter of Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant on Thursday, Iranian state media reported, citing Ehsan Jahanian, deputy governor of Bushehr province. Jahanian said several areas across the province were targeted, including the area around the nuclear plant, a military base in the town of Choghadak and a fishing pier in southern Bushehr. He said there were no immediate reports of casualties. Residents in Choghadak, located just over 20km (12 miles) from the Bushehr plant, reported hearing several explosions. The Bushehr facility, Iran’s only civilian nuclear power plant, has previously been affected by strikes in the area during the ongoing Middle East war.

items.title: Iran warns of retaliation if IAEA adopts resolution against Tehran
items.summary: Iran warns of retaliation if IAEA adopts resolution against Tehran Iran has warned that it will take reciprocal action if the UN nuclear watchdog adopts a resolution against Tehran, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on Monday. Speaking at a press briefing, Baghaei criticised European states seeking a resolution against Iran, calling their approach “irrational” given that the ongoing US-Iran war has made several Iranian nuclear facilities inaccessible to international inspectors. His comments come as the US, Britain, France and Germany push for a resolution at the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) over Iran’s lack of cooperation and access to its nuclear sites. Iran has restricted IAEA access to facilities affected by previous strikes, arguing that normal safeguarding arrangements have become impractical under wartime conditions. The dispute has deepened concerns over the status of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile and the international community’s ability to verify the nature of its nuclear programme.
